title: Write a clean-up composition with controlled sentence variety
instructions: Composition practice. The prompt: ‘Write about an activity your class did to help the community.’ You are writing about your class's clean-up of the river path behind the school. Your notes: 24 students from Form 2B cleaned the path on a Saturday morning; the leader gave each pair a map of one section, so no part of the path was cleaned twice; heavy rain started at 10 a.m., so the group stopped half an hour early; the leader called everyone back to the school gate; the students filled 31 bags; most bags held plastic bottles; the caretaker collected the bags at the gate. Choose the sentences you would write. Answer all six questions before viewing feedback.

parts.prompt: You want to open with who did what. Which option is a complete sentence?

options.text: Twenty-four students from Form 2B cleaned the river path behind the school on Saturday.
Although twenty-four students from Form 2B cleaned the river path behind the school on Saturday.
Twenty-four students from Form 2B cleaning the river path behind the school on Saturday.
Twenty-four students from Form 2B, who cleaned the river path behind the school on Saturday.

choice_rationales.A: It has a subject, ‘twenty-four students’, and a verb showing tense, ‘cleaned’, so it can stand alone.
choice_rationales.B: ‘Although’ makes the clause dependent, and no main clause follows.
choice_rationales.C: ‘Cleaning’ does not show tense, so there is no complete verb.
choice_rationales.D: The ‘who’ clause describes the students, but the sentence has no main verb.

parts.hint: Look for a subject and a verb showing tense, with no word that makes the clause depend on another.
parts.correct_explanation: A complete sentence names who did the action and gives a verb that shows tense.

parts.prompt: You want one sentence that shows why the group stopped early. Which should you write?

options.text: Heavy rain started at 10 a.m., the group stopped half an hour early.
Because heavy rain started at 10 a.m., the group stopped half an hour early.
Because heavy rain started at 10 a.m., so the group stopped half an hour early.
Heavy rain started at 10 a.m., although the group therefore stopped half an hour early.

choice_rationales.A: A comma alone cannot join two complete clauses, so this is a comma splice.
choice_rationales.B: ‘Because’ makes the rain the reason and attaches it to a complete main clause.
choice_rationales.C: ‘Because’ and ‘so’ mark the same link twice.
choice_rationales.D: ‘Although’ signals a contrast and ‘therefore’ a result, so the link is confused.

parts.hint: Use one linking word that makes the first fact the reason for the second.
parts.correct_explanation: One linking word such as ‘because’ shows the cause clearly and avoids both a comma splice and a doubled link.

parts.prompt: You have started a sentence with ‘When the leader gave each pair a map of one section,’. Which version is complete and keeps to the notes?

options.text: When the leader gave each pair a map of one section.
When the leader gave each pair a map of one section, and the path.
When the leader gave each pair a map of one section, no part of the path was cleaned twice.
When the leader gave each pair a map of one section, cleaning only their own part of the path.

choice_rationales.A: The ‘when’ clause still leaves the reader waiting for the main idea.
choice_rationales.B: The words after the comma are not a complete clause.
choice_rationales.C: The main clause completes the sentence and reports what the notes record.
choice_rationales.D: The ‘-ing’ group has no subject or verb showing tense, so the sentence is still incomplete.

parts.hint: A ‘when’ clause needs a complete main clause after it.
parts.correct_explanation: A dependent opening adds variety only when a complete main clause follows it.

parts.prompt: You want to say that every pair had a map and what that achieved. Which sentence is correct and clear?

options.text: Each of the pairs were given a map, and this helped them with it.
Each pair was given a map of one section, so no part of the path was cleaned twice.
Each pair was given it, and this made it a lot easier for them.
Each of the pairs have a map, which proves that every clean-up will always succeed.

choice_rationales.A: ‘Each’ is singular, so it needs ‘was’; ‘this’, ‘them’ and ‘it’ are unclear.
choice_rationales.B: ‘Each pair’ agrees with ‘was’, and the second clause names the result.
choice_rationales.C: The verb agrees, but ‘it’ and ‘this’ do not point to anything named.
choice_rationales.D: ‘Each’ needs ‘has’, and the claim about every clean-up goes beyond the notes.

parts.hint: Find the main noun of the subject, then make sure every pronoun points to something named.
parts.correct_explanation: Combined sentences must keep subject–verb agreement and name the action and result clearly.

parts.prompt: Which THREE sentences could you use? Each must be complete and use its structure to show a clear link or emphasis.

options.text: When the rain grew heavy, the leader called everyone back to the gate.
Although most of the bags held plastic bottles.
The bags were heavy, they were carried to the gate.
The students carried the bags to the school gate, where the caretaker collected them.
Each of the students were given a pair of gloves.
The students filled 31 bags. Most held plastic bottles.

choice_rationales.A: The time clause is attached to a complete main clause and shows the order of events.
choice_rationales.B: The ‘although’ clause has no main clause, so it is a fragment.
choice_rationales.C: Two complete clauses are joined only by a comma.
choice_rationales.D: The ‘where’ clause adds a linked detail to a complete main clause.
choice_rationales.E: ‘Each’ is singular and needs ‘was’; the notes also do not mention gloves.
choice_rationales.F: Both sentences are complete, and the short second sentence gives the key finding emphasis.

parts.hint: Check that each sentence is complete and correct before judging what its pattern adds.
parts.correct_explanation: Variety can come from a time clause, a ‘where’ clause or a short sentence for emphasis, as long as every sentence is complete.

parts.prompt: Which paragraph would be the best one to write, with varied sentences that stay correct?

options.text: Cleaning the river path on Saturday. Twenty-four students came, the leader gave out maps. Because of the rain at ten. Filling bags and carrying them. Most of them bottles, which the caretaker.

Twenty-four students from Form 2B cleaned the river path behind the school on Saturday. Because each pair had a map of one section, no part of the path was cleaned twice. Heavy rain started at 10 a.m., so the leader called everyone back half an hour early. The students had filled 31 bags. Most held plastic bottles.

Twenty-four students from Form 2B cleaned the river path on Saturday, and each pair had a map, and no part was cleaned twice, and heavy rain started at 10 a.m., and the leader called everyone back, and the students had filled 31 bags, and most held plastic bottles, and the caretaker collected all of them at the school gate.

Although twenty-four students cleaned the path. Each of the pairs were given a map, it stopped them cleaning it twice. Heavy rain started, therefore the path called everyone back, which proves the clean-up was perfect because they filled them.

choice_rationales.A: Fragments and a comma splice stop the facts from forming complete, controlled sentences.
choice_rationales.B: Varied structures each show a real link or give emphasis, and agreement and reference stay clear.
choice_rationales.C: Joining everything with ‘and’ makes one overloaded sentence and gives every idea the same weight.
choice_rationales.D: The opening is a fragment, ‘each’ does not agree with ‘were’, the pronouns are unclear and the claim is too strong.

parts.hint: Choose the paragraph whose varied patterns show cause, order and emphasis without grammar or reference errors.
parts.correct_explanation: Useful variety follows the logic of the paragraph: the structure changes because the link or the emphasis changes.
